rules.sentence: Initial treatment consists of corticosteroids, intravenous gamma globulin, or anti-D immunoglobulin in patients who are Rh posi-tive.
Platelet transfusions are not usually needed unless cen-tral nervous system bleeding or active bleeding from other sites occurs.
Secondary immune thrombocytopenia often presents with a very low platelet count, petechiae and pur-pura, and epistaxis.
In children, it is usually acute in onset, short lived, and typically follows a viral illness.
In contrast, ITP in adults is gradual in onset, chronic in nature, and has no identifiable cause.
Because the circulating platelets in ITP are young and functional, bleeding is less for a given platelet count than when there is failure of platelet production.

Shortened platelet survival is seen in immune thrombocytopenia, disseminated intravascular coagu-lation, or disorders characterized by platelet thrombi such as thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura and hemolytic uremic syndrome.
